explain: In Chinese, four (四) sounds like the word for death, so I've set aside arrangements of four stems. I'm happy to make any of them with five.
White chrysanthemums are kept for mourning in Chinese and Japanese custom, so I've left out the arrangement built around them.
Arrangements made for mourning stay out of every other occasion.
In many Hindu families white leans towards mourning, so for a happy occasion I've chosen colour instead.
Bright reds and oranges are colours of celebration, so I've kept them away from a message of sympathy.
Bright and red flowers are out of place at a wake, so I've kept to white, green and soft tones.
At a wake a standing wreath is customary. What I make here is best sent to the family home; if you need a wreath, tell me and I'll arrange one.
For a Chinese family in mourning, white and soft green are the customary colours, so I've put those first.
In Malay Muslim custom flowers are less usual at the funeral itself. A simple arrangement sent to the family home after the burial is a gentle way to show you care.
Many wards don't allow plants in soil, and in Japanese custom a potted plant suggests a long stay, so I've left those out.
Heavy pollen and strong scent can trouble patients and their neighbours, so I've left those out.
Some wards don't allow fresh flowers at all. Crochet is welcome anywhere, and it comes home with them.
Camellias fall whole from the stem, which in Japanese custom makes them unlucky for someone unwell.
Because of allergies, I've left out anything with heavy pollen or scent.
Crochet has no pollen at all, so I've brought it forward.
Lilies are toxic to cats, even the pollen, so they're out.
